claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: 10–20% of ALMR neurons stimulated by high-level expression of mCherry produce an exopher.
claims.source: Previous work showed that 10–20% of ALMR neurons stimulated by high-level expression of mCherry produce an exopher (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Arnold et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: If an ALMR neuron produces an exopher, it generally only produces a single such vesicle in its lifetime.
claims.source: If an ALMR neuron produces an exopher, it generally only produces a single such vesicle in its lifetime, with most exophers produced on day 2 of adulthood (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Arnold et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Most exophers are produced on day 2 of adulthood.
claims.source: with most exophers produced on day 2 of adulthood (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Arnold et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Very few exophers appear outside of the day 1 to day 3 timeframe.
claims.source: Very few exophers appear outside of the day 1 to day 3 timeframe, which correlates with the high metabolic activity associated with reproduction, and an organismal switch in overall proteostatic stress response (Labbadia and Morimoto, 2014; Morimoto, 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Exophers in the ALMR neuron typically emerge from the neuronal soma in a polarized manner, formed from the plasma membrane opposite the large neurite.
claims.source: Exophers in the ALMR neuron typically emerge from the neuronal soma in a polarized manner, formed from the plasma membrane opposite the large neurite (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Arnold et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: As a budded exopher moves away from the soma it initially remains connected to the soma by a thin thread-like nanotube.
claims.source: as a budded exopher moves away from the soma it initially remains connected to the soma by a thin thread-like nanotube (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Arnold et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The exopher quickly breaks up into smaller vesicles referred to as 'starry night' (SN) vesicles, which later disappear.
claims.source: The exopher quickly breaks up into smaller vesicles that we refer to as 'starry night' (SN) vesicles, which later disappear (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Arnold et al., 2020; Figure 1A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and Figure 1A showing the progression.

claims.claim: Exophers appear most frequently on adult day 2 (D2), with fewer appearing on adult day 1 (D1) or adult day 3 (D3).
claims.source: As previously described, exophers appear most frequently on adult day 2 (D2), with fewer appearing on adult day 1 (D1) or adult day 3 (D3), and very few appearing outside of this age range (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Arnold et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The vast majority of mCherry-filled exophers convert into smaller 'starry night' (SN) vesicles before the eventual loss of the neuronal exopher-derived mCherry signal.
claims.source: We noted that the vast majority of mCherry-filled exophers convert into smaller 'starry night' (SN) vesicles, and this always precedes the eventual loss of the neuronal exopher-derived mCherry signal (Figure 1A–C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by longitudinal tracking data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Exopher-derived small vesicles often appeared within the first 2 hr after exopher formation.
claims.source: Exopher-derived small vesicles often appeared within the first 2 hr after exopher formation (D1 mean = 2.0 hr [N = 32], D2 mean = 2.5 hr [N = 22])
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from longitudinal tracking experiments.

claims.claim: All detectable exopher-derived mCherry signal was lost over the course of 3–4 days.
claims.source: Most exophers were eventually fully converted to starry night vesicles, with all detectable exopher-derived mCherry signal lost over the course of 3–4 days (D1 mean persistence = 80 hr [N = 24], D2 mean persistence = 98 hr [N = 14])
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from longitudinal tracking experiments.

claims.claim: A minor fraction (7%) of exophers did not convert to starry night vesicles and persisted over a 7-day tracking period.
claims.source: A minor fraction of exophers did not convert to starry night vesicles (7%, N = 118). These exophers persisted and were never degraded over a 7-day tracking period
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from longitudinal tracking experiments.

claims.claim: There is an obligatory transition from large exopher to smaller starry night vesicles prior to eventual degradation of exopher contents in the hypodermis.
claims.source: Taken together our results suggest an obligatory transition from large exopher to smaller starry night vesicles prior to eventual degradation of exopher contents in the hypodermis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the longitudinal tracking data showing the sequence of events.

claims.claim: Most exophers examined (74%) were clearly coated in hypodermal F-actin.
claims.source: We found that most exophers we examined were clearly coated in hypodermal F-actin (74% positive, N = 27)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: The hypodermal membrane around the neuronal soma was not enriched in F-actin.
claims.source: while the hypodermal membrane around the neuronal soma was not enriched in F-actin (Figure 2A and B)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: Most intact exophers (65%) were surrounded by hypodermal puncta positive for mNG::PH(PLCδ), a biosensor for the lipid PI(4,5)P2.
claims.source: We also noted that most (65%, n = 45) intact exophers were surrounded by hypodermal puncta positive for mNG::PH(PLCδ), a biosensor for the lipid PI(4,5)P2, with significantly more PI(4,5)P2 signal overlap with the exopher periphery than the nearby neuronal soma periphery (Figure 2C and D; Lemmon et al., 1995)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: PI(4,5)P2 is typically enriched on the phagocytic cup and is removed rapidly upon phagosome sealing.
claims.source: PI(4,5)P2 is typically enriched on the phagocytic cup and is removed rapidly upon phagosome sealing (Botelho et al., 2000)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and is established knowledge.

claims.claim: Hypodermal F-actin was not yet apparent when the neuronal bud first started to emerge in 5/6 captured budding events, but F-actin was eventually acquired in all cases.
claims.source: In 5/6 cases, hypodermal F-actin was not yet apparent when the neuronal bud first started to emerge, but in all cases F-actin was eventually acquired, indicating hypodermal recognition and engulfment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2E and Video 2.

claims.claim: Depletion of hypodermal actin using tissue-specific RNAi against actins act-1, act-2, or act-3 resulted in accumulation of exophers.
claims.source: we found that depletion of hypodermal actin using tissue-specific RNAi against actins act-1, act-2, or act-3 resulted in accumulation of exophers derived from the ALMR neuron, suggesting a failure in hypodermal phagocytosis (Figure 2F)
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Hypodermis-specific depletion of arx-2 resulted in the accumulation of exophers and a reduction in starry night vesicles.
claims.source: Hypodermis-specific depletion of arx-2, encoding the Arp2 subunit of the Arp2/3 complex required for formation of branched actin during phagocytosis (Goley and Welch, 2006), also resulted in the accumulation of exophers and a reduction in starry night vesicles that derive from exopher degradation (Figure 2G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: A canonical actin-dependent hypodermal phagocytosis response is initiated in response to extruded exophers.
claims.source: our data support the interpretation that a canonical actin-dependent hypodermal phagocytosis response is initiated in response to extruded exophers
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the actin and Arp2/3 data.

claims.claim: Hypodermally expressed mNeonGreen markers for distinct steps of phagosomal maturation label the periphery of intact ALMR neuron-derived exophers, but this labeling was weak.
claims.source: We found that hypodermally expressed mNeonGreen markers for distinct steps of phagosomal maturation label the periphery of intact ALMR neuron-derived exophers, but this labeling was weak, further supporting the interpretation that large exophers are usually associated with early stages of hypodermal phagocytosis (Figure 3A–H)
claims.evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Intact exophers show frequent weak labeling for early phagosome marker RAB-5 (42%, N = 29).
claims.source: we noted frequent weak labeling for early phagosome marker RAB-5 (42%, N = 29)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: Intact exophers show frequent weak labeling for late phagosome marker RAB-7 (70%, N = 24).
claims.source: late phagosome marker RAB-7 (70%, N = 24)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: Intact exophers show weak labeling for autophagosome marker LGG-1/LC3.
claims.source: and autophagosome marker LGG-1/LC3, suggesting that hypodermal early endosomes, late endosomes, and autophagosomes begin to associate with large phagocytosed exophers (Figure 3A–F)
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: Early and late phagosome marker labeling, and autophagosome marker labeling, is much more pronounced after fragmentation of the exopher-laden phagosome.
claims.source: Notably, however, early and late phagosome marker labeling, and autophagosome marker labeling, is much more pronounced later, after fragmentation of the exopher-laden phagosome (Figure 4A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Little acquisition of hypodermally expressed lysosome marker LMP-1/LAMP by intact exopher-phagosomes was observed.
claims.source: We observed little acquisition of hypodermally expressed lysosome marker LMP-1/LAMP by intact exopher-phagosomes, suggesting little lysosome association at the large single phagosome exopher stage (Figure 3G and H)
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claims.claim: Starry night vesicles show very little colocalization with Golgi marker AMAN-2.
claims.source: we found very little colocalization of starry night vesicles with Golgi marker AMAN-2 or basolateral recycling endosome marker RME-1 (Figure 4A and B)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Starry night vesicles show very little colocalization with basolateral recycling endosome marker RME-1.
claims.source: we found very little colocalization of starry night vesicles with Golgi marker AMAN-2 or basolateral recycling endosome marker RME-1 (Figure 4A and B)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Starry night vesicles show strong colocalization with hypodermally expressed 2XFYVE(HRS), a biosensor for the early phagosomal lipid PI(3)P.
claims.source: our quantitative imaging documented strong colocalization of starry night vesicles with hypodermally expressed 2XFYVE(HRS), a biosensor for the early phagosomal lipid PI(3)P; RAB-10, a recycling regulator associated with early phagosomes and endosomes; and RAB-7, a marker of late phagosomes and endosomes (Figure 4A and B; Levin et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Starry night vesicles show strong colocalization with RAB-10, a recycling regulator associated with early phagosomes and endosomes.
claims.source: RAB-10, a recycling regulator associated with early phagosomes and endosomes
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Starry night vesicles show strong colocalization with RAB-7, a marker of late phagosomes and endosomes.
claims.source: and RAB-7, a marker of late phagosomes and endosomes (Figure 4A and B; Levin et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Starry night vesicles show strong colocalization with LGG-1/LC3, a canonical marker of autophagosomes.
claims.source: We also found strong colocalization with LGG-1/LC3, a canonical marker of autophagosomes, recently found to contribute to phagosomal cargo degradation in C. elegans (Figure 4A and B; Peña-Ramos et al., 2022)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Starry night vesicles reflect exopher-laden early and late phagosomes that have undergone vesiculation.
claims.source: We conclude that starry night vesicles reflect exopher-laden early and late phagosomes that have undergone vesiculation
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the marker colocalization data.

claims.claim: Multilamellar vesicles within the hypodermis near the ALMR neuron were identified by electron microscopy in exopher-producing animals but not control animals.
claims.source: By electron microscopy, we identified multilamellar vesicles within the hypodermis near the ALMR neuron. These vesicles appeared in exopher-producing animals but not control animals, appearing similar to phagosome vesiculation products.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The multilamellar vesicles measured 200–500 nm in size, significantly smaller than the average extruded large vesicle exopher (~3 μm).
claims.source: The vesicles measured 200–500 nm in size, significantly smaller than the average extruded large vesicle exopher (~3 μm)
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy measurements.

claims.claim: In cup-5 mutants, colocalization of exopher-derived vesicles with the LMP-1 lysosome marker was greatly increased.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, in cup-5 mutants colocalization with the LMP-1 lysosome marker was greatly increased, the size of starry night vesicles was significantly larger, and the average fluorescence intensity of mCherry in starry night vesicles was significantly higher (Figure 5A–D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claims.claim: In cup-5 mutants, the size of starry night vesicles was significantly larger.
claims.source: the size of starry night vesicles was significantly larger
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In cup-5 mutants, the average fluorescence intensity of mCherry in starry night vesicles was significantly higher.
claims.source: the average fluorescence intensity of mCherry in starry night vesicles was significantly higher (Figure 5A–D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Most exopher-derived material taken up by the hypodermis from the neuron is degraded in hypodermal phagolysosomes.
claims.source: Our results suggest that most exopher-derived material taken up by the hypodermis from the neuron is degraded in hypodermal phagolysosomes
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cup-5 mutant data showing accumulation when lysosome function is impaired.

claims.claim: Lysosome fusion is a late step in exopher processing.
claims.source: and that lysosome fusion is a late step in exopher processing
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the timing of LMP-1 marker acquisition.

claims.claim: Lysosome function was not required for the transition from large exopher-containing phagosome into starry night phagosome fragments.
claims.source: Lysosome function was not required for the transition from large exopher-containing phagosome into starry night phagosome fragments.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cup-5 mutant data showing vesiculation still occurs.

claims.claim: Loss of sand-1 caused a significant increase in the detection of intact exopher-laden phagosomes, along with loss of most smaller starry night fragmented phagosomes.
claims.source: we found that loss of sand-1 caused a significant increase in the detection of intact exopher-laden phagosomes, along with loss of most smaller starry night fragmented phagosomes (Figure 5E and F)
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: Conversion from a large exopher-laden phagosome to smaller starry night phagosomal fragments is important for cargo degradation.
claims.source: We conclude that conversion from a large exopher-laden phagosome to smaller starry night phagosomal fragments is important for cargo degradation
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the sand-1 mutant data.

claims.claim: The molecular changes associated with early to late phagosome maturation, such as loss of RAB-5 and acquisition of GTP-bound RAB-7, are required for fragmentation into starry night vesicles.
claims.source: and that the molecular changes associated with early to late phagosome maturation, such as loss of RAB-5 and acquisition of GTP-bound RAB-7, are required for fragmentation into starry night vesicles.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the sand-1 mutant data and the known role of SAND-1 in RAB-7 activation.

claims.claim: arl-8 hypomorphic mutants exhibit a defect in transitioning from large exopher-laden phagosomes to smaller starry night phagosomal vesicles.
claims.source: We found that arl-8 hypomorphic mutants exhibit a defect in transitioning from large exopher-laden phagosomes to smaller starry night phagosomal vesicles.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: cnt-1 and rab-35 mutants accumulate large intact exophers.
claims.source: We found that cnt-1 and rab-35 mutants accumulate large intact exophers, with higher levels of exophers present until at least day 4 of adulthood in cnt-1 mutants, by which point nearly all WT exophers are normally consumed (Figure 6D, G, and H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Hypodermis-specific expression of CNT-1::mNG or mNG::RAB-35, but not touch-neuron-specific expression, rescued exopher and starry night numbers in their respective mutants.
claims.source: we find that hypodermis-specific expression of CNT-1::mNG or mNG::RAB-35, but not touch-neuron-specific expression, rescued exopher and starry night numbers in their respective mutants (Figure 6H and I)
claims.evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 6H and I.

claims.claim: CNT-1 and RAB-35 function in the hypodermis for exopher clearance.
claims.source: This tissue-specific rescue indicates that CNT-1 and RAB-35 function in the hypodermis for exopher clearance (Figure 6M)
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific rescue data.

claims.claim: Hypodermis-specific mNG::RAB-35 could be clearly visualized labeling the periphery of large exophers (N = 12), but not around the neuronal soma.
claims.source: Hypodermis-specific mNG::RAB-35 could be clearly visualized labeling the periphery of large exophers (N = 12), but not around the neuronal soma, as predicted for a direct role in exopher clearance (Figure 6B)
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Hypodermis-specific CNT-1::GFP often labeled exophers more than somas (N = 22), but was found in characteristic puncta at the exopher periphery rather than labeling the periphery smoothly like RAB-35.
claims.source: Hypodermis-specific CNT-1::GFP also often labeled exophers more than somas (N = 22), but was found in characteristic puncta at the exopher periphery rather than labeling the periphery smoothly like RAB-35 (Figure 6A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: RAB-35 and CNT-1 have a direct role in regulating hypodermal phagosome formation during neuronal exopher processing.
claims.source: Taken together, our results support a direct role for RAB-35 and CNT-1 in regulating hypodermal phagosome formation during neuronal exopher processing.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the localization and mutant data.

claims.claim: arf-6 mutants had significantly reduced exopher numbers in ALMR neurons expressing mCherry or GFP.
claims.source: we found a significant reduction in exopher numbers in arf-6 mutants in ALMR neurons expressing mCherry or GFP (Figure 6D, E, and J)
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: arf-6 mutants lacked most starry night, indicating that the loss of exophers was not due to an increased rate of hypodermal processing.
claims.source: Furthermore, arf-6 mutants lacked most starry night, indicating that the loss of exophers was not due to an increased rate of hypodermal processing (Figure 6J)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: daf-2; arf-6 double mutants showed a pronounced loss of exophers and starry night phagosomes.
claims.source: This experiment confirmed a pronounced loss of exophers and starry night phagosomes in arf-6 mutants (Figure 6K)
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 6K.

claims.claim: Similar rates of small bud production were found in both daf-2 and daf-2; arf-6 double mutants.
claims.source: we found similar rates of small bud production in both genotypes, suggesting that very early events in exophergenesis in arf-6 mutants occur at normal frequency (Figure 6—figure supplement 4; Videos 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-lapse video analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and Videos 3 and 4.

claims.claim: ARF-6 is important for exopher production, likely affecting small bud growth to form the large exopher bud, or to prevent regression of exopher buds once formed.
claims.source: Our results indicate that ARF-6 is important for exopher production, likely affecting small bud growth to form the large exopher bud, or to prevent regression of exopher buds once formed.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the time-lapse data showing normal bud initiation but reduced exopher completion.

claims.claim: Re-expression of arf-6(+) in just the hypodermis in the arf-6(Δ) background rescued exopher and starry night numbers.
claims.source: re-expression of arf-6(+) in just the hypodermis in the arf-6(Δ) background rescued exopher and starry night numbers (Figure 6J)
claims.evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: arf-6 depletion via hypodermis-specific RNAi conferred the same reduction in exopher and starry night numbers as the arf-6(Δ) mutants.
claims.source: arf-6 depletion via hypodermis-specific RNAi conferred the same reduction in exopher and starry night numbers as the arf-6(Δ) mutants (Figure 7A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: ARF-6 activity in the hypodermis facilitates the successful production of exophers in the neuron.
claims.source: Both lines of testing support the interpretation that ARF-6 activity in the hypodermis facilitates the successful production of exophers in the neuron.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific rescue and RNAi data.

claims.claim: A higher level of hypodermal ARF-6::mNeonGreen puncta was associated with the exopher periphery than around the neuronal soma.
claims.source: We also measured a higher level of hypodermal ARF-6::mNeonGreen puncta associated with the exopher periphery than around the neuronal soma, supporting the idea of a direct role for hypodermal ARF-6 in promoting neuronal exopher production (Figure 6C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The elevated number of exophers found in cnt-1 and rab-35 mutants was suppressed in cnt-1;arf-6 and rab-35;arf-6 double mutants.
claims.source: We found that the elevated number of exophers found in cnt-1 and rab-35 mutants was suppressed in cnt-1;arf-6 and rab-35;arf-6 double mutants (Figure 6G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: RAB-35 and CNT-1 act as negative regulators of ARF-6.
claims.source: This is consistent with RAB-35 and CNT-1 acting as negative regulators of ARF-6.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis data.

claims.claim: An arf-6(ns388) gain-of-function mutant produced increased exopher numbers, similar to rab-35 and cnt-1 mutants.
claims.source: we found that an arf-6(ns388) gain-of-function mutant (Kutscher et al., 2018) produced increased exopher numbers, similar to rab-35 and cnt-1 mutants, and the opposite of the arf-6 loss-of-function mutants (Figure 6F)
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: rab-35 mutant exopher accumulation could be partly rescued by hypodermal CNT-1 overexpression.
claims.source: we found that rab-35 mutant exopher accumulation could be partly rescued by hypodermal CNT-1 overexpression, while cnt-1 mutant exopher accumulation was not rescued by RAB-35 overexpression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
claims.evidence: This is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: cnt-1 mutant exopher accumulation was not rescued by RAB-35 overexpression.
claims.source: while cnt-1 mutant exopher accumulation was not rescued by RAB-35 overexpression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
claims.evidence: This is supported by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Greater association of ARF-6::mNeonGreen with exophers was found in cnt-1 mutants than wild-type controls.
claims.source: We also found greater association of ARF-6::mNeonGreen with exophers in cnt-1 mutants than wild-type controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 3)
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: RAB-35 upregulates CNT-1, and CNT-1 downregulates ARF-6 via ARF-GAP activity within the hypodermal cell.
claims.source: Taken together, these results are consistent with a model in which RAB-35 upregulates CNT-1, and CNT-1 downregulates ARF-6 via ARF-GAP activity within the hypodermal cell (Figure 6M)
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis and overexpression data.

claims.claim: Only knockdown of sec-10 produced an overall phenotype similar to arf-6, with significantly reduced exopher and starry night frequency.
claims.source: Among these, we found that only knockdown of sec-10, a component of the vesicle tethering complex Exocyst, produced an overall phenotype similar to arf-6, with significantly reduced exopher and starry night frequency (Figure 7D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAi screening data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: ARF-6 and SEC-10 function together in the hypodermis in a process required for the neuron to efficiently produce exophers.
claims.source: Our data suggest that ARF-6 and SEC-10 function together in the hypodermis in a process required for the neuron to efficiently produce exophers.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similar phenotypes of arf-6 mutants and sec-10 RNAi.

claims.claim: Hypodermis-specific RNAi of ppk-1 reduced starry night frequency, but did not reduce the number of exophers.
claims.source: Hypodermis-specific RNAi of ppk-1 reduced starry night frequency, but did not reduce the number of exophers, which is different from arf-6 and sec-10 phenotypes (Figure 7B)
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Hypodermis-specific depletion of ppk-1 produced higher than normal numbers of exophers remaining attached to the neuronal soma.
claims.source: We also noted that hypodermis-specific depletion of ppk-1 produced higher than normal numbers of exophers remaining attached to the neuronal soma and measured a similar defect in arf-6 mutants for the few exophers that are produced without ARF-6 (Figure 6L and Figure 7G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6L and Figure 7G.

claims.claim: PPK-1 participates in the exopher engulfment process downstream of ARF-6, but only in the later phase required for phagosome release (sealing).
claims.source: we propose that PPK-1 participates in the exopher engulfment process downstream of ARF-6, but only in the later phase required for phagosome release (sealing), since ppk-1 knockdown only phenocopies the later part of the arf-6 mutant phenotype (Figure 6L and Figure 7A, D)
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of ppk-1 and arf-6 disruption.

claims.claim: ARF-6 has dual roles, one early in exopher recognition/interaction by the hypodermis, and another role later in hypodermal phagosome completion.
claims.source: Our data may indicate dual roles for ARF-6, one early in exopher recognition/interaction by the hypodermis, and another role later in hypodermal phagosome completion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the multiple phenotypes observed in arf-6 mutants.

claims.claim: ced-1 mutants had significantly reduced exopher and starry night numbers, similar to the effects observed in arf-6 mutants and sec-10 hypodermis-specific knockdown.
claims.source: We found that ced-1 mutants had significantly reduced exopher and starry night numbers, similar to the effects we observed in arf-6 mutants and sec-10 hypodermis-specific knockdown (Figure 8A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: ced-1 mutant exopher production was rescued by hypodermis-specific re-expression of CED-1.
claims.source: Furthermore, ced-1 mutant exopher production was rescued by hypodermis-specific re-expression of CED-1, indicating a hypodermal focus for these CED-1 effects (Figure 8B)
claims.evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: ttr-52 and anoh-1 mutants display strongly reduced levels of exopher production similar to ced-1 mutants.
claims.source: We found that ttr-52 and anoh-1 mutants display strongly reduced levels of exopher production similar to ced-1 mutants (Figure 8D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: PS exposure contributes to exopher recognition.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that PS exposure contributes to exopher recognition
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ttr-52 and anoh-1 mutant data.

claims.claim: A specific engulfing cell interaction with the neuron strongly influences the eventual production of the exopher itself.
claims.source: and further suggest that a specific engulfing cell interaction with the neuron strongly influences the eventual production of the exopher itself.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ced-1, ttr-52, and anoh-1 mutant data.

claims.claim: Hypodermal CED-1ΔC::GFP clearly labeled the periphery of exophers undergoing engulfment.
claims.source: Indeed, hypodermal CED-1ΔC::GFP clearly labeled the periphery of exophers undergoing engulfment.

results.result: Exophers undergo an obligatory transition to smaller 'starry night' vesicles before degradation. Longitudinal tracking showed that the vast majority of mCherry-filled exophers convert to starry night vesicles within ~2 hours, with complete degradation occurring over 3-4 days. A small fraction (7%) failed to convert and persisted indefinitely.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are well-supported by longitudinal tracking data presented in Figure 1, with quantitative measurements of timing (N=32 for D1, N=22 for D2) and persistence (N=24 for D1, N=14 for D2). The obligatory nature of the transition is demonstrated by the high frequency (93%) of conversion and the consistent temporal sequence observed.

results.result: Exophers undergo actin-dependent phagocytosis by the surrounding hypodermis. Most exophers (74%) were coated in hypodermal F-actin, while neuronal somas were not. Exophers also accumulated PI(4,5)P2, a phagocytic cup marker. Hypodermis-specific depletion of actin or Arp2/3 resulted in exopher accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C53 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence including quantitative imaging (N=27 for F-actin, N=45 for PI(4,5)P2), time-lapse microscopy (6 budding events captured), and tissue-specific RNAi experiments (Figure 2). The data consistently demonstrate canonical phagocytic machinery involvement.

results.result: Intact exophers show weak labeling for early phagosome maturation markers. Intact exophers displayed weak labeling for RAB-5 (42%), RAB-7 (70%), and LGG-1/LC3, with little LMP-1 lysosome marker acquisition. Marker labeling became much more pronounced after exopher fragmentation into starry night vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 are supported by quantitative confocal imaging data (Figure 3) with appropriate sample sizes (N=13-29 depending on marker). The weak labeling of intact exophers contrasts with strong labeling of fragmented vesicles, supporting the interpretation that phagosome maturation accelerates after vesiculation.

results.result: Starry night vesicles represent maturing phagosomes containing exopher-derived cargo. These vesicles showed minimal colocalization with Golgi or recycling endosome markers but strong colocalization with early phagosome markers (2XFYVE, RAB-10), late phagosome markers (RAB-7), and autophagosome markers (LGG-1/LC3).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are well-supported by comprehensive marker colocalization analysis (Figure 4A-B) with appropriate sample sizes (N=12-30 depending on marker). The pattern of marker association is consistent with phagosome identity and maturation, and the conclusion (C66) logically follows from the data.

results.result: Electron microscopy identified multilamellar vesicles in the hypodermis near ALMR neurons in exopher-producing animals. These vesicles measured 200-500 nm, significantly smaller than intact exophers (~3 μm), consistent with phagosome vesiculation products.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 4C) showing multilamellar vesicles specifically in exopher-producing animals. The size measurements and morphology are consistent with the starry night vesicles observed by fluorescence microscopy, providing ultrastructural validation.

results.result: Lysosome function is required for exopher content degradation but not for phagosome vesiculation. In cup-5 lysosome mutants, colocalization with LMP-1 increased, starry night vesicles were larger, and mCherry intensity was higher, but vesiculation still occurred.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by quantitative analysis of cup-5 mutants (Figure 5A-D) with appropriate sample sizes (N=17 WT, N=20 mutant). The data clearly distinguish between vesiculation (which occurs) and degradation (which is impaired), supporting the conclusion that lysosome fusion is a late step.

results.result: SAND-1/Mon1-mediated phagosome maturation is required for exopher-phagosome fragmentation. Loss of sand-1 caused accumulation of intact exopher-phagosomes and loss of starry night vesicles, persisting through day 4 of adulthood. This indicates that RAB-5 to RAB-7 conversion is required for fragmentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by sand-1 mutant analysis (Figure 5E-F) showing a clear processing-stalled phenotype. The interpretation that RAB-7 activation is required for fragmentation is reasonable given SAND-1's known role as a RAB-7 exchange factor, though direct RAB-7 involvement is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: ARL-8 hypomorphic mutants exhibit defects in transitioning from large exopher-phagosomes to starry night vesicles, suggesting a role for kinesin-mediated motor activity in phagosome vesiculation.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by arl-8 mutant analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing delayed vesiculation. The phenotype is less pronounced than sand-1, consistent with hypomorphic rather than null alleles. The kinesin connection is reasonable given ARL-8's known function but represents an inference.

results.result: CNT-1 and RAB-35 function in the hypodermis to regulate exopher clearance. Both cnt-1 and rab-35 mutants accumulated intact exophers. Hypodermis-specific, but not neuron-specific, expression rescued the phenotype. Both proteins localized to exopher peripheries.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 are strongly supported by mutant analysis, tissue-specific rescue experiments (Figure 6H-I), and localization data (Figure 6A-B). The tissue-specific rescue provides compelling evidence for hypodermal function (N=12 for RAB-35, N=22 for CNT-1 localization).

results.result: ARF-6 is required for exopher production, likely affecting bud growth or preventing bud regression. arf-6 mutants showed significantly reduced exopher and starry night numbers. Time-lapse analysis revealed normal small bud frequency but reduced exopher completion.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89 are supported by multiple experimental approaches including mutant analysis in different backgrounds (Figure 6D-E, K), time-lapse video analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, Videos 3-4), and quantitative measurements. The interpretation that ARF-6 affects bud growth rather than initiation is well-supported by the time-lapse data.

results.result: ARF-6 functions in the hypodermis to facilitate neuronal exopher production. Hypodermis-specific re-expression of arf-6 rescued exopher numbers, as did hypodermis-specific RNAi depletion. Hypodermal ARF-6 was enriched at exopher peripheries compared to neuronal somas.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 are strongly supported by tissue-specific rescue experiments (Figure 6J), hypodermis-specific RNAi (Figure 7A), and localization data (Figure 6C, N=24). This represents a key finding that hypodermal factors influence neuronal exopher production, a non-cell-autonomous effect.

results.result: RAB-35 and CNT-1 act as negative regulators of ARF-6 in a genetic pathway. Double mutant epistasis analysis showed arf-6 suppressed cnt-1 and rab-35 phenotypes. An arf-6 gain-of-function mutant phenocopied cnt-1 and rab-35 mutants. CNT-1 overexpression partially rescued rab-35 but not vice versa.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 are supported by comprehensive genetic epistasis experiments (Figure 6F-G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2-3). The data consistently support a pathway where RAB-35 upregulates CNT-1, which downregulates ARF-6. The ordering is well-established through multiple complementary experiments.

results.result: SEC-10/exocyst functions with ARF-6 in the hypodermis for neuronal exopher production. Among candidate ARF-6 effectors tested, only sec-10 knockdown produced a phenotype similar to arf-6, with reduced exopher and starry night frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by hypodermis-specific RNAi screening (Figure 7D). The specificity of the sec-10 phenotype among multiple candidates tested strengthens the conclusion. The interpretation that ARF-6 and SEC-10 function together is reasonable given SEC-10's role in vesicle tethering.

results.result: PPK-1 participates in late-stage exopher engulfment downstream of ARF-6. Hypodermis-specific ppk-1 RNAi reduced starry night but not exopher numbers, and increased soma-attached exophers, similar to a subset of arf-6 phenotypes. This suggests ARF-6 has dual roles in early recognition and late phagosome completion.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by RNAi data (Figure 7B, G) and comparison with arf-6 phenotypes (Figure 6L). The interpretation of dual ARF-6 roles is reasonable given the partial phenocopy by ppk-1, though this represents an inference from the differential effects observed.

results.result: CED-1 phagocytic receptor, TTR-52, and ANOH-1 are required in the hypodermis for efficient neuronal exopher production. All three mutants showed reduced exopher and starry night numbers. Hypodermis-specific CED-1 re-expression rescued the phenotype. This suggests PS exposure contributes to exopher recognition and that phagocyte interaction influences exopher production.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 are supported by mutant analysis (Figure 8A, D), tissue-specific rescue (Figure 8B), and the known roles of these proteins in PS recognition. The conclusion that phagocyte interaction influences exopher production is well-supported, representing a key non-cell-autonomous finding.

results.result: CED-1 specifically labels exopher buds but not attached neuronal somas. Hypodermal CED-1ΔC::GFP clearly labeled exopher peripheries and became enriched at early budding sites while excluding the soma. This pattern is attributed to CED-1 recruitment by exopher-surface signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are supported by imaging data (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The striking specificity of CED-1 localization to exophers versus somas provides strong evidence for differential surface signals. The interpretation of signal-mediated recruitment is reasonable given constitutive CED-1 expression.

results.result: CED-10/Rac is required for completing exopher phagocytosis but not for exopher generation. ced-10 mutants and hypodermis-specific RNAi accumulated exophers with reduced starry night vesicles. Hypodermal CED-10 was enriched around exophers compared to somas.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by mutant/RNAi analysis (Figure 8E-F) and localization data (Figure 8G). The differential effect compared to CED-1/ARF-6/SEC-10 (accumulation vs. reduction) clearly distinguishes CED-10's role in phagocytosis execution rather than exopher generation.

results.result: Two classes of phagocytic regulators exist: those required for neuronal exopher production (CED-1, ARF-6, SEC-10) and those required only for phagocytosis execution (CED-10, actin, Arp2/3). This distinction reveals that phagocyte recognition influences exopher generation in the neuron.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120 represent a synthesis of multiple experimental results showing differential effects of various phagocytic regulators. The classification is well-supported by the contrasting phenotypes: reduced exophers (CED-1, ARF-6, SEC-10) versus accumulated exophers (CED-10, actin, Arp2/3). This is a key conceptual advance.

results.result: The hypodermis engulfs exophers via defined phagocytosis steps and processes them through phagosome maturation, ultimately degrading neuron-derived cargo in phagolysosomes. This represents the overall fate of exophers after release from neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C122 summarize the major findings of the study, which are supported by extensive experimental evidence including marker studies, mutant analysis, and electron microscopy. This represents the central conclusion integrating multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: arf-6 and ced-1 mutants show reduced touch sensitivity at day 10 but not day 5 of adulthood, indicating deficits in old-age neuronal function when exopher maturation is compromised.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C145 are supported by touch sensitivity assays (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) with appropriate replication (3 biological replicates, 30 animals each). The age-specific effect strengthens the interpretation of functional consequences, though causality to exopher defects specifically cannot be definitively established.

results.result: Hypodermal recognition is required for neuronal exopher production, not just clearance. arf-6 and ced-1 mutants showed reduced exopher production that was rescued by hypodermis-specific re-expression. In contrast, actin/Arp2/3/CED-10 depletion accumulated exophers. Time-lapse data suggest hypodermal recognition is required for bud elaboration or preventing bud regression.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C135 are supported by mutant analysis, tissue-specific rescue, and time-lapse imaging. The distinction between factors affecting exopher production versus clearance is well-established. The interpretation about bud elaboration/regression is reasonable given normal early bud frequency in arf-6 mutants.

results.result: Hypodermal CED-1 distinguishes between exopher and soma, revealing likely asymmetry in surface membrane components. CED-1 accumulated around exopher buds but not neuronal somas, even at early budding stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 are supported by CED-1 localization data (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The inference of membrane asymmetry is reasonable and important for understanding the mechanism of selective recognition. This represents a key mechanistic insight.

results.result: RAB-35 and CNT-1 mutants allow exopher production but block phagosome completion, potentially through effects on PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3)P levels required for recruiting fission factors. High external forces may be required to complete phagocytosis given the nanotube connection between soma and exopher.
results.evaluation: Claim C146 is supported by mutant data. However, C147 and C148 are largely speculative, based on prior literature about lipid requirements and nanotube observations. While reasonable hypotheses, these mechanisms are not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: Exopher phagocytosis differs mechanistically from linker cell phagocytosis. While both involve RAB-35/CNT-1/ARF-6, arf-6 single mutants have no effect on linker cells but strong effects on exophers. Additionally, linker cell phagocytosis is CED-1 independent unlike exopher phagocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C155 are supported by comparison with prior literature (Kutscher et al., 2018) and the current findings. The mechanistic differences are clearly established through the differential genetic requirements, highlighting context-dependent phagocytosis mechanisms.

results.result: ARF-6 and SEC-10/exocyst may control CED-1 recycling for early exopher recognition, and ARF-6 has an additional later role with PPK-1 in phagosome completion. Exophers in arf-6 mutants were more likely to remain soma-attached, similar to ppk-1 depletion.
results.evaluation: Claim C156 is speculative, proposing a mechanism for CED-1 recycling that is not directly tested. Claim C157 is supported by data (Figure 6L, Figure 7G), but the interpretation of dual ARF-6 roles, while reasonable, represents an inference from phenotypic observations rather than direct mechanistic demonstration.

results.result: Exopher-phagosome resolution resembles phagosomal resolution in C. elegans embryos and mammalian macrophages. Recent work implicates Rab7-effector ORPL1 and ER tethering in mammalian systems. ARL-8 requirement suggests kinesin motor activity drives exopher-phagosome tubulation and fragmentation.
results.evaluation: Claim C158 is supported by comparison with prior literature. C159 accurately cites prior work. C160 is supported by arl-8 mutant data and is a reasonable inference given ARL-8's known role in recruiting kinesins, though the specific motor involvement is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: LGG-1/LC3 acquisition by fragmented but not intact exopher-phagosomes suggests autophagosome fusion rather than LC3-associated phagocytosis. The order of events differs from macrophages where lysosome fusion precedes fragmentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C163 are supported by LGG-1 and LMP-1 localization data (Figures 3-4). The interpretation favoring autophagosome fusion over LC3-associated phagocytosis is reasonable given the timing of LGG-1 acquisition. The comparison with macrophages is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Close interplay between exopher-ejecting cells and phagocytes may be conserved across species. Mouse cardiomyocytes maintain dedicated macrophages for exopher acceptance. The mechanism resembles neuronal pruning by glia and polyglutamine aggregate transfer in Drosophila. PS exposure likely contributes to recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C138, C140, and C141 appropriately cite prior literature for comparative context. C139 is speculative about conservation but reasonable. C142 is supported by ttr-52 and anoh-1 mutant data and established CED-1 function. These claims provide important evolutionary and mechanistic context.

results.result: Removal of exopher contents by phagocytosis is likely neuroprotective, based on prior work showing better neuronal function in exopher-producing neurons and the current findings of age-dependent functional deficits in exopher-processing mutants.
results.evaluation: Claim C143 is inferred from prior work (Melentijevic et al., 2017) and the touch sensitivity data (C144-C145). While the inference is reasonable, the current study does not directly demonstrate neuroprotection, and the authors acknowledge caveats about the specificity of ARF-6 and CED-1 to exophergenesis.

results.result: Conserved roles for CED-1/Draper in aggregate extrusion underscore potential importance of mammalian MEGF10-dependent mechanisms in pathological aggregate spread and invite focus on glial phagocytosis partners in addressing neuropathology.
results.evaluation: Claim C164 appropriately synthesizes findings across C. elegans and Drosophila (with citations) to suggest mammalian relevance. C165 is speculative about future research directions but reasonable given the findings. These represent appropriate translational implications of the work.

results.result: Background and context about exophers, neuronal proteostasis, and the C. elegans touch neuron system. Exophers are giant vesicles produced by stressed neurons that can carry aggregates and organelles. The C. elegans ALMR touch neuron is the best-studied system, producing exophers primarily on day 2 of adulthood.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C39, C123-C129) provide established background from prior literature and general knowledge. They are appropriately cited and accurately represent the field's understanding. These contextual claims frame the current study but are not primary findings.
